title: The Advisor You Forgot to Invite 2026
author: Jeremy Utley
source: 1-Minute Wednesday No. 331, Greg McKeown newsletter (gregmckeown.com), November 11,
summary: This week's 1-Minute Wednesday is a guest post by Jeremy Utley, introduced by Greg McKeown, arguing that AI's greatest value is helping you ask better questions at the moment a decision is forming. Utley describes turning down a keynote that would have cost him his daughter's birthday-morning donut tradition, a choice he made only because he happened to remember a story from Essentialism. He then asked an AI assistant how Greg McKeown would think about the decision and got a sharper restatement of the trade-off. Citing Marquet and Gillespie's idea of distancing and Andy Grove's 1985 'walk out the door' moment at Intel, he argues that a decision-maker needs an outside perspective. His practical advice is a two-prompt sequence: ask the AI how a named advisor would think about the decision, then give it the details and ask for the implications, treating the answer as a question rather than a verdict.
points: The biggest obstacle to a wise decision is usually being too close to it, and an invited outside perspective can make a hard call obvious.
AI assistants that have absorbed an advisor's published work can be asked to reason as that advisor would, before you commit to a yes.
The measure of progress is shortening the 'time to forehead slap', the gap between struggling and remembering you can ask for help.
A two-prompt sequence (how would this person think, then here are the details) turns AI into a question-raiser rather than a decision-maker.
quotes: In the book Distancing, former submarine captain David Marquet and psychologist Michael Gillespie argue that the biggest obstacle to a wise decision is usually the person making it. We are too close.
Same facts. Same two men. One new person in the room, and an impossible decision became obvious.
Most of us don't have a Gordon Moore. We do have something stranger.
We have an assistant open on our screens all day that has read everything our best advisors ever published. We ask it for drafts and summaries. Almost nobody asks it to be someone.
The thinking didn't disappear when the tool did the production. It moved to evaluation (Lee et al., 2025).
The goal isn't to stop slapping your forehead. It's to slap it sooner.
That was never the hard part. The hard part is remembering to ask it while the yes is still forming.
It is a question, not a verdict. You are not asking it to decide for you. You are asking it to make sure the right question gets asked before you do.
